g.text: 333,000 writes/sec is not the workload. 13.3 million pushes/sec is.
Every decision here is about making one inbound update become 40 outbound pushes as cheaply as possible.
Same question as the proximity service - inverted in every dimension that matters
ONLY FRIENDS - a social graph gates every read
rebuild constantly - or don't index at all
expires in minutes - a stale position is useless
A restaurant is written once and read a million times, so you index it heavily and query the index. A person is written every
30 seconds and read by about 40 people - the write:read ratio is INVERTED, and any index that is expensive to update is
disqualified. Which is why there is NO SPATIAL INDEX ANYWHERE on the hot path: a conclusion that looks like an omission until
you see the numbers. Distance is a pairwise computation between two known points, 40 times per update.
One update in, forty pushes out - and the sender never learns who is listening
each server, for each of ITS clients
end. Filtering at the sender would
mean the sender's server needs every
40x the write rate. A design that
The structural move, and what it avoids
A client's server subscribes to the channels of that client's
friends. An update is published to ONE channel - the sender's -
and delivery is the pub/sub layer's problem.
You do not need to know who is listening. Each server tracks
only its own clients' subscriptions, which is local state it
already has. Nothing global is consulted on the hot path.
the alternative: a global 'who is connected where' registry
The sender's server looks up the friend list, finds where each friend is connected, and
sends 40 targeted messages. That requires a global registry consulted on EVERY update -
333,000 lookups/sec, each returning 40 rows - and rewritten on every connect and
disconnect, for 10 million connections that churn constantly.
Publishing to your own channel inverts the problem: instead of the sender finding the
listeners, the listeners find the sender, once, at subscribe time.
'Occasional dropped points are acceptable' is the most load-bearing requirement in the design
no retry queues, no dead-letter handling.
an in-memory cache with a TTL
rather than a replicated database - and TTL
expiry doubles as the 'friends inactive for
a restart may drop in-flight updates
and nobody has to reconcile anything
If a location update were durable-or-bust, every one of 333,000/sec would need an acknowledged, replicated write - a
WALLET-GRADE durability requirement applied to data that is worthless in 30 seconds. But the next update arrives in 30
seconds and corrects everything, so: SELF-CORRECTING DATA DOES NOT NEED DURABILITY. Recognising which data has that property
is what separates this design from an over-engineered one.
Sizing the pub/sub cluster: two estimates pointing in opposite directions
100M pre-allocated channels x ~2 KB = 205 GB -> 2 nodes
So the cluster is sized entirely by PUSH THROUGHPUT and the memory is incidental - it is CPU-bound, not memory-bound, which
is the opposite of most cache-cluster sizing. Two more numbers worth separating: the live location cache is 10M x ~100 bytes
= about 1 GB, trivial and bounded by the TTL rather than by growth; while location HISTORY is 333,000 rows/sec retained
forever at ~40 bytes = 1.15 TB/DAY. That is not the live feature - it is an append-only analytics stream with completely
different requirements, which is why it lives in a different store.
And the 30-second refresh is not an arbitrary constant: at a walking speed of 1.4 m/s a person moves ~42 m in 30 s, well
inside any useful radius - so anything faster multiplies the 13.3M number for no user-visible benefit.
